ingredients.item: beef short ribs, flanken-cut across the bone, 8–10 mm thick, lightly crosshatch scored
/2 Asian pear , grated and squeezed nearly dry
Steamed rice , lettuce ssam, cold oi muchim and kimchi — the fresh, cold banchan matters more here, the ribs run hot

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: Charcoal or cast-iron at medium-hot — you can hold your hand over it 3–4 seconds. The gochujang sugars scorch faster than soy marinade, so build a cool zone or keep the grate a hand higher than for #M03. Bone side down first, single layer.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the paste should sizzle quietly and smell toasted-chile-sweet, not burnt. Any black smoke in the first minute means the fire is too close — raise the grate before the first flip, not after the first casualty.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Grill 3–4 minutes a side. The visual law changes in this lane: you are not waiting for mahogany, you are waiting for the red paste to darken one shade toward brick and go glossy at the edges. Flip once at the weep; pull the strip when the cut edge at the bone shows no raw red.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the pull test: brick-red lacquer, glossy, light char in the score marks, meat firm at the bone with a pink sliver allowed. Eat one piece at the grill station — the heat should land after the sweet, never before it.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Scissors to single-bone pieces, warm platter, sesame over, straight into ssam with rice and a piece of cold cucumber banchan in the same bite's orbit.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: eating test: sweet, then warm heat, then beef — and the cold oi muchim resets the palate between ssam. If the heat erases the beef, the gochujang ran over 80 g; weigh it next time.

storageNotes: Marinated ribs keep 24 hours. Cooked, 3 days — chop off the bone into fried rice or a quesadilla, where the residual lacquer does the seasoning. Bones to the stock pot.

Variations: the soy-pear parent (#M03); pork shoulder in this same paste is the spicy dwaeji bulgogi record (#M13); thinned with a splash of water and a spoon of vinegar, the leftover paste becomes a brushable glaze for grilled shrimp (#SF01).
